name: Mpra
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Mprɛ language' (en), accessed 2026-09-17; and Glottolog 5.x languoid page mpra1235 (Note: 'There is a small amount of data on a now extinct enigmatic language of Ghana'; refs Blench 1999, 2007, 2012; Goody 1963; Campbell et al. 2022 for AES 'extinct')
sources.note: Neither says anything about phonology, tone or stress; Wikipedia states knowledge of the language derives from a 70-word list in a 1931 article and gives the name pronunciation [ḿpœ̩ɛ̀]. Used only to build the bibliography (Cardinall 1931, Goody 1963, Painter 1967, Blench 1999/2007/2012).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2015 [printout 6 Jan 2015]. Recovering data on Mpra [=Mpre] a possible language isolate in North-Central Ghana. Draft circulated for comment. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 9 pp. (current rogerblench.info file Language/Niger-Congo/Kwa/)
sources.note: Nothing. A reformatted reprint of the 2007 draft (new address block only); a line diff against the 2007 text shows no added content. No mention of stress, accent or tone.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2012. Niger-Congo: an alternative view. Ms., Cambridge: KWEF.
sources.note: Classification paper cited by Wikipedia/Glottolog for Mpra as a divergent Kwa branch; classification-only, very unlikely to contain a stress statement.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2007 [printout 12 Jan 2007]. The Dompo language of Central Ghana and its affinities. Draft circulated for comment. 16 pp.
sources.note: downloaded to chase the Glottolog/Wikipedia item Blench 1999 'Report on Dompo and a note on Mpre'. This Dompo wordlist does not mention Mpre/Mpra at all; its sec. 3.3 Tones (p. 5: 'The tone system of Dompo is quite restricted with only two tones') concerns Dompo only. Not a Mpra source; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2007. Recovering data on Mpra [=Mpre] a possible language isolate in North-Central Ghana. Draft circulated for comment, printout 10 March 2007. Cambridge: Mallam Dendo. 10 pp. (Glottolog ref 109374)
sources.note: Nothing. Wordlist-recovery paper: Table 1 (pp. 3-5) reproduces ~110 orthographic items from Cardinall 1931 and Goody 1963 with no tone or stress marks; Table 2 (p. 7) gives 14 proverb openings recorded in 2007, 'run together in modern pronunciation, so the exact word division is guesswork' (p. 6). The words stress, accent, tone, prosody, syllable, phonology do not occur anywhere in the text.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 1999. Recent field work in Ghana: report on Dompo and a note on Mpre. Ms., formerly hosted on the Lyon CLHASS 'Isolats' page.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Glottolog-listed item; per Blench 2007 it predates any new Mpra data, so expected to be silent on stress, but it is the only Glottolog reference not seen.

sources.citation: Goody, J.R. 1963. Ethnological notes on the distribution of the Guang languages. Journal of African Languages 2(3): 173-189.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Second and last first-hand Mpre wordlist (recorded Dec. 1956 from the last knowledgeable inhabitant); would confirm whether any phonetic/prosodic remark exists. Not online; HathiTrust may hold it search-only.

sources.citation: Cardinall, A.W. 1931. A survival. Gold Coast Review 5(1): 193-197.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only primary record of Mpre while it was still spoken (~70-word list plus ethnographic note); the sole place an early observer might have remarked on pronunciation, though Blench's reproduction of its items shows no tone/stress marking.

sources.citation: Painter, Colin. 1967. The distribution of Guang in Ghana, and a statistical pre-testing on twenty-five idiolects. Journal of West African Languages 4(1): 25-78.
sources.note: Open scan downloaded from journalofwestafricanlanguages.org but it has no text and the page scan are only 340x508 px (144 ppi); one-process tesseract scanned at 150 dpi produced unreadable output (22 KB for 54 pp., no hit for Mpre/Gonja/Nnyamase), so the paper could not actually be read. Wikipedia cites it only for the ethnonym Nnyamase-mprɛ having become Nnyamase-Gonja; it is a Guang survey, not a Mpra description.
